claims.text: Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C promotes nanoscale precipitation.
The nanoscale precipitates have a thermal expansion coefficient significantly different from that of the BCC matrix.
Differential thermal expansion between precipitates and the BCC matrix generates localized internal residual stresses.
The mismatch-induced residual stresses modify dislocation mobility, including glide and climb dynamics.
Internal residual stresses modify lattice dynamics.
Changes in dislocation behavior affect yield strength and hardening.
Changes in dislocation mobility affect creep rates in HfNbTaTiZr at 1250 °C.
Mismatch-induced residual stresses affect the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
Compared with quenched HfNbTaTiZr, aged samples will have increased yield strength.
Aged samples will exhibit greater hardening in post-cold-rolling microhardness tests than quenched samples.
Aged samples will show altered elastic-modulus trends over 293–1100 K relative to quenched samples.
The altered elastic-modulus trends will correlate with the measured thermal-expansion mismatch.
Aged samples will have lower tensile creep rates at 1250 °C than quenched samples.
Rapid quenching can produce a homogenized, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy with suppressed prior precipitation.
The quenched baseline will have a uniform BCC matrix, uniform thermal-expansion behavior, and lower internal residual stresses.
Controlled aging at 600–800 °C induces microsegregation in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed comparison applies to aging at 600–800 °C, elastic-modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K, and creep testing at 1250 °C.

The mechanism would be falsified if aged and quenched samples show no statistically significant mechanical or elastic differences and no measurable residual-stress mismatch consistent with differential thermal expansion.
